title: "Integrals"
engine: julia
---

```{julia}
#| echo: false
using ConvolutionInterpolations, CairoMakie, Printf, Random
```

A negative `derivative` order gives an interpolant of an integral: `derivative = -1` is the
antiderivative, `-2` the twofold integral, and so on. Like the derivatives, integrals are
evaluated analytically from the kernel's polynomial pieces, not by quadrature, and they are
anchored at the first knot: there the integral is zero, and so are all lower integrals. So the
antiderivative evaluated at $b$ is $\int_{x_0}^{b}$ of the interpolant, and a definite integral
between two limits is the difference of two evaluations.

In the Julia package an integral can be evaluated in two ways, and the choice is between speed
and memory. By default (`fast = true`) the contribution of the knots left of the stencil is
precomputed and stored when the interpolant is built, so an evaluation costs the same whatever
the size of the grid. With `fast = false` nothing is stored beyond the data, and every
evaluation sums over the knots up to the stencil instead: the cost of an evaluation then grows
with the grid, but the interpolant needs no extra memory. The two agree to rounding. The
[section below](#fast-or-low-memory) shows when each is the better choice.

## A first example

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Julia

```{julia}
x = range(0, 2π, length = 40)                             # 40 uniformly spaced samples
y = sin.(x)                                               # the values at the samples
i1 = convolution_interpolation(x, y; derivative = -1)     # the integral from x[1] = 0
i2 = convolution_interpolation(x, y; derivative = -2)     # the twofold integral, also anchored at 0

a, b = 1.0, 2.5                                           # the limits of a definite integral
i1(1.0), i2(1.0), i1(b) - i1(a)                           # 1 − cos(1), 1 − sin(1), cos(a) − cos(b)
```

## Python

```python
import numpy as np
from convinterp import convolution_interpolation

x = np.linspace(0.0, 2 * np.pi, 40)                       # 40 uniformly spaced samples
y = np.sin(x)                                             # the values at the samples
i1 = convolution_interpolation(x, y, derivative=-1)       # the integral from x[0] = 0
i2 = convolution_interpolation(x, y, derivative=-2)       # the twofold integral, also anchored at 0

a, b = 1.0, 2.5                                           # the limits of a definite integral
i1(1.0), i2(1.0), i1(b) - i1(a)                           # 1 − cos(1), 1 − sin(1), cos(a) − cos(b)
```

:::

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
println("| | ∫₀¹ f | ∫₀¹∫₀ˢ f | ∫ₐᵇ f |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|--:|")
@printf("| interpolant | %.12f | %.12f | %.12f |\n", i1(1.0), i2(1.0), i1(b) - i1(a))
@printf("| exact | %.12f | %.12f | %.12f |\n", 1 - cos(1.0), 1 - sin(1.0), cos(a) - cos(b))
```

## Integrals don't cost convergence order

Where each derivative order costs one order of convergence, integrals cost none: the integral
of the interpolant converges at least as fast as the interpolant itself. Runge's function with
`:b7`, the interpolant and its first and second integrals:

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "The convergence study"
runge(x) = 1 / (1 + 25x^2)                                # Runge's function
irunge = (x -> (atan(5x) + atan(5)) / 5,                  # its integral from −1
          x -> (x * (atan(5x) + atan(5)) - log(1 + 25x^2) / 10 + log(26) / 10) / 5)  # its twofold integral from −1
xr = range(-1, 1, length = 2001)                          # fine points for measuring the error
ns = [41, 81, 161, 321, 641, 1281]                        # the numbers of samples
hs = 2 ./ (ns .- 1)                                       # the corresponding spacings
orders = 0:-1:-2                                          # the interpolant and two integrals
exact = (runge, irunge...)                                # the function and its integrals

errors = [begin
              xn = range(-1, 1, length = n)
              itp_m = convolution_interpolation(xn, runge.(xn); kernel = :b7, derivative = m)
              maximum(abs.(itp_m.(xr) .- exact[1-m].(xr)))
          end for n in ns, m in orders]

fig = Figure(size = (800, 420))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xscale = log10, yscale = log10, xreversed = true,
          xlabel = "spacing h", ylabel = "largest error")
for (j, m) in enumerate(orders)
    scatterlines!(ax, hs, max.(errors[:, j], 1e-17); markersize = 8,
                  label = m == 0 ? "interpolant" : "integral order $(-m)")
end
Legend(fig[1, 2], ax)
fig
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
observed = [begin
                e = errors[:, j]
                i = findlast(v -> v > 1e-13, e); i = max(i, 2)   # the finest grid still clear of rounding
                log(e[i-1] / e[i]) / log(hs[i-1] / hs[i])
            end for j in eachindex(orders)]
println("| | interpolant | integral order 1 | integral order 2 |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|--:|")
println("| observed convergence order | ", join((@sprintf("%.2f", o) for o in observed), " | "), " |")
```

Each kernel supports integrals up to a fixed order: 2 for `:a0` and `:a1`, 4 for the other
`:a` kernels, 6 for `:b5` and 8 for `:b7` to `:b13`.

## Fast or low memory

With the default, `fast = true`, evaluating an integral costs about the same as evaluating the
interpolant, whatever the number of knots: the contribution of every knot left of the stencil
is a polynomial in the position within the cell, and those polynomials are precomputed and
stored when the interpolant is built. The stored tables grow with the integral order and with
the number of integrated axes, so high orders in several dimensions cost memory. With
`fast = false` the tables are left out, and each evaluation sums over the knots between the
anchor and the stencil instead. The same twofold integral along both axes of a 400 × 400 grid,
built both ways:

```{julia}
xm = range(0, 2π, length = 400)                           # knots along x
ym = range(0, 2π, length = 400)                           # knots along y
dm = [sin(xi) * cos(yi) for xi in xm, yi in ym]           # sin(x)·cos(y) on the grid

i_fast = convolution_interpolation((xm, ym), dm; derivative = (-2, -2))                # the default: tables stored
i_lean = convolution_interpolation((xm, ym), dm; derivative = (-2, -2), fast = false)  # nothing stored beyond the data

i_fast(4.0, 5.0), i_lean(4.0, 5.0)                        # the same integral: (4 − sin 4)·(1 − cos 5)
```

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "The timings and sizes"
using Chairmarks                                          # the benchmarking package

# Write a time in seconds with a unit that suits its size
function readable_time(t)
    if t < 1e-6
        return @sprintf("%.0f ns", 1e9 * t)                 # below a microsecond: nanoseconds
    elseif t < 1e-3
        return @sprintf("%.1f μs", 1e6 * t)                 # below a millisecond: microseconds
    else
        return @sprintf("%.1f ms", 1e3 * t)                 # otherwise milliseconds
    end
end

build_fast = (@b convolution_interpolation((xm, ym), dm; derivative = (-2, -2))).time                # time to build with tables
build_lean = (@b convolution_interpolation((xm, ym), dm; derivative = (-2, -2), fast = false)).time  # time to build without
eval_fast = (@b i_fast(4.0, 5.0)).time                    # time of one evaluation with tables
eval_lean = (@b i_lean(4.0, 5.0)).time                    # time of one evaluation without
size_fast = Base.summarysize(i_fast) / 2^20               # memory held by the interpolant, in MiB
size_lean = Base.summarysize(i_lean) / 2^20               # the same without the tables
nothing                                                   # the table below shows the results
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
println("| | value at (4, 5) | construction | one evaluation | memory |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|")
@printf("| `fast = true` | %.12f | %s | %s | %.1f MiB |\n", i_fast(4.0, 5.0), readable_time(build_fast), readable_time(eval_fast), size_fast)
@printf("| `fast = false` | %.12f | %s | %s | %.1f MiB |\n", i_lean(4.0, 5.0), readable_time(build_lean), readable_time(eval_lean), size_lean)
```

The cost of each option follows a simple rule. With integral orders $m_1, \dots, m_n$ along
the $n$ integrated axes, the default holds

$$
\prod_{i=1}^{n} (1 + m_i)
$$

arrays the size of the data: one is the data itself, and the other $\prod_i (1 + m_i) - 1$ are
the stored tables. One evaluation costs the same on any grid.
With `fast = false` there is one array, the data, and one evaluation sums over the knots
between the anchor and the point along the integrated axes, so its cost is proportional to the
number of knots in that box. In the example above both orders are 2, which makes
$(1 + 2)(1 + 2)$ arrays against one. Three axes at the highest order of the `:b7` kernel would
need $(1 + 8)^3$ arrays the size of the data; that is where `fast = false` is the option that
remains. The tables are stored for at most three integrated axes: with four or more, every
evaluation sums over the knots, whatever `fast` is set to.

So the default suits an integral that is evaluated many times, and `fast = false` suits a few
evaluations on a large dataset, or orders and dimensions whose tables would not fit in memory.

## Integrals in more dimensions

In more dimensions the orders are given per axis, and integrals combine freely with
interpolation and derivatives along the other axes. The antiderivative along every axis is the
iterated integral from the corner of the grid; a derivative along one axis and an integral
along another is a Leibniz-rule operator, in one evaluation:

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Julia

```{julia}
xg = range(0, 2π, length = 60)                            # knots along x
yg = range(0, 2π, length = 60)                            # knots along y
data = [sin(xi) * cos(yi) for xi in xg, yi in yg]         # sin(x)·cos(y) on the grid

ixy = convolution_interpolation((xg, yg), data; derivative = (-1, -1))   # ∫∫ from (0, 0)
ix  = convolution_interpolation((xg, yg), data; derivative = (-1, 0))    # ∫ dx, interpolated in y
dxiy = convolution_interpolation((xg, yg), data; derivative = (1, -1))   # ∂/∂x ∫ dy

ixy(1.0, 2.0), ix(1.0, 2.0), dxiy(1.0, 2.0)
```

## Python

```python
xg = np.linspace(0.0, 2 * np.pi, 60)                      # knots along x
yg = np.linspace(0.0, 2 * np.pi, 60)                      # knots along y
data = np.sin(xg)[:, None] * np.cos(yg)[None, :]          # sin(x)·cos(y) on the grid

ixy = convolution_interpolation((xg, yg), data, derivative=(-1, -1))    # ∫∫ from (0, 0)
ix  = convolution_interpolation((xg, yg), data, derivative=(-1, 0))     # ∫ dx, interpolated in y
dxiy = convolution_interpolation((xg, yg), data, derivative=(1, -1))    # ∂/∂x ∫ dy

ixy(1.0, 2.0), ix(1.0, 2.0), dxiy(1.0, 2.0)
```

:::

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
println("| at (1, 2) | ∫₀¹∫₀² f | ∫₀¹ f dx | ∂/∂x ∫₀² f dy |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|--:|")
@printf("| interpolant | %.12f | %.12f | %.12f |\n", ixy(1.0, 2.0), ix(1.0, 2.0), dxiy(1.0, 2.0))
@printf("| exact | %.12f | %.12f | %.12f |\n", (1 - cos(1.0)) * sin(2.0), (1 - cos(1.0)) * cos(2.0), cos(1.0) * sin(2.0))
```

## Discontinuous data

The `:a0` kernel, which is nearest-neighbour interpolation, integrates piecewise-constant data
exactly: a spike one cell wide and $1/h$ high integrates to a unit step, which is how a
sampled impulse should behave.

```{julia}
n = 1001                                                  # knots
xs = range(0, 2π, length = n)
h = step(xs)                                              # the spacing
spike = [abs(xi - π) < h / 2 ? 1 / h : 0.0 for xi in xs]  # a unit-area spike at π
F = convolution_interpolation(xs, spike; kernel = :a0, derivative = -1)   # its integral

xf = range(0, 2π, length = 801)
fig = Figure(size = (800, 400))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "x")
lines!(ax, xf, F.(xf); label = "∫ spike")
lines!(ax, xf, (xf .> π) .* 1.0; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, label = "unit step")
Legend(fig[1, 2], ax)
fig
```

## Nonuniform and scattered data

The examples above are on uniform grids, which is what a negative `derivative` needs. Data
that are not on a uniform grid are integrated in the Julia package in one of two ways, and
which one fits depends on the data: resampling a nonuniform interpolant on a uniform grid, for
trusted data on a nonuniform grid, or the scattered-data fit, for noisy data and for data that
are not on a grid at all. In the Python package, integrals are for uniform grids for now.

### Trusted data on a nonuniform grid

The [nonuniform kernels](nonuniform.qmd) keep their high order on any grid, so trusted data on
a nonuniform grid are best interpolated with them first. That interpolant has no antiderivative
of its own, but it can be evaluated on a uniform grid fine enough to carry it, and the result
integrated. Runge's function on jittered knots, uniform knots each moved by a random fraction
of the spacing:

```{julia}
Random.seed!(1)                                           # the same jitter at every render
nj = 81                                                   # the number of knots
hj = 2 / (nj - 1)                                         # their average spacing on [-1, 1]
xj = collect(range(-1, 1, length = nj))                   # start from uniform knots
xj[2:end-1] .+= 0.3hj .* (rand(nj - 2) .- 0.5)            # move the inner ones by up to 15 % of the spacing
yj = runge.(xj)                                           # Runge's function at the jittered knots

itp_j = convolution_interpolation(xj, yj; kernel = :b7)   # the nonuniform interpolant
xu = range(-1, 1, length = 2nj - 1)                       # a uniform grid, twice as fine on average
ij = convolution_interpolation(xu, itp_j.(xu); derivative = -1)   # resampled and integrated from −1

ij(0.0), ij(1.0)                                          # atan(5)/5 and 2·atan(5)/5
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
println("| | ∫ from −1 to 0 | ∫ from −1 to 1 |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|")
@printf("| interpolant | %.12f | %.12f |\n", ij(0.0), ij(1.0))
@printf("| exact | %.12f | %.12f |\n", irunge[1](0.0), irunge[1](1.0))
```

### Noisy or scattered data

Measured data usually carry noise, and scattered points are not on a grid, so neither suits
the nonuniform kernels. The [scattered-data fit](scattered.qmd) takes the samples as points
and returns an interpolant on a uniform grid of its own, smoothed by default with the amount
of smoothing chosen automatically, and that interpolant takes a negative `derivative`
directly. The integral is anchored at the first knot of the fit's grid, which is the leftmost
sample. Runge's function measured with noise at random positions:

```{julia}
Random.seed!(2)                                           # the same samples at every render
np = 200                                                  # the number of samples
xp = 2 .* rand(np) .- 1                                   # random positions on [-1, 1]
yp = runge.(xp) .+ 0.01 .* randn(np)                      # Runge's function, measured with noise

pts = reshape(xp, 1, :)                                   # the samples as points: a matrix, one column each
ip = convolution_interpolation(pts, yp; derivative = -1)  # smoothing fit, integrated from the leftmost sample

x0 = minimum(xp)                                          # the anchor of the integral
ip(0.0), ip(0.5)                                          # the integrals from x0 to 0 and to 0.5
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
println("| | ∫ from x₀ to 0 | ∫ from x₀ to 0.5 |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|")
@printf("| interpolant | %.6f | %.6f |\n", ip(0.0), ip(0.5))
@printf("| exact | %.6f | %.6f |\n", irunge[1](0.0) - irunge[1](x0), irunge[1](0.5) - irunge[1](x0))
```

The fit has to stay on its default uniform grid for an integral, since `grid = :adaptive` gives
a nonuniform interpolant. For trusted scattered data, `mode = :exact` interpolates the points
instead of smoothing them. The [scattered data page](scattered.qmd) has the details and an
integral over a box of scattered points in two dimensions.
